title: Contact
text:
MELANOBS is coordinated by Thomas Ibanez, a research fellow at the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD) and a member of the AMAP lab. He is based in Nouméa, New Caledonia.
Thomas is a vegetation ecologist whose main interest is to understand how tree communities are shaped in tropical island forests and how they respond to global change. He works mostly in New Caledonia and across Melanesia. Within MELANOBS, he coordinates the regional network of partners and leads the permanent plots in New Caledonia.
Email: thomas.ibanez@ird.fr

title: News
text:
September 2026

MELANOBS presented at the 11th Pacific Islands Conference on Nature Conservation
Thomas Ibanez presented the MELANOBS project during a Species Working Group session of the 11th Pacific Islands Conference on Nature Conservation and Protected Areas, held at the Tjibaou Cultural Centre in Nouméa, New Caledonia (7–11 September 2026).






September 2026

Vanuatu National Herbarium team trained in Nouméa
The team of the Vanuatu National Herbarium (PVNH) spent a week in Nouméa for herbarium management training. They also took part in the resurvey of the Great Ferns Provincial Park plot, and are now ready to resurvey the Nusumetu plot back in Vanuatu.






July 2026

New permanent plot at Vago, Fiji
MELANOBS partners from the Fiji Ministry of Forestry, the University of the South Pacific and the AMAP lab set up a new 1-ha permanent forest plot at Vago, on the island of Viti Levu, Fiji. See the Vago plot page.






March 2026

First resurvey of the Blue River Provincial Park plot
The MELANOBS team completed the first resurvey of the Blue River Provincial Park plot, one year after it was set up. Trees grew slowly overall, except in and around the large gap.






December 2025

First resurvey of the Siloam plot
The MELANOBS team completed the first resurvey of the Siloam plot, one year after it was set up. Trees grew very slowly.






September 2025

New permanent plot at Great Ferns, New Caledonia
The MELANOBS team set up a new 1-ha permanent forest plot in the Great Ferns Provincial Park, on the island of Grande Terre, New Caledonia. Kagus (Rhynochetos jubatus) joined the party! See the Great Ferns Provincial Park plot page.






May 2025

New permanent plot at Poitete, Solomon Islands
MELANOBS partners from Solomon Islands National University, the Solomon Islands Ministry of Forestry and Research and the AMAP lab set up a new 1-ha permanent forest plot at Poitete, on the island of Kolombangara, Solomon Islands. See the Poitete plot page.






March 2025

New permanent plot at Blue River, New Caledonia
The MELANOBS team set up a new 1-ha permanent forest plot in the Blue River Provincial Park, on the island of Grande Terre, New Caledonia. See the Blue River Provincial Park plot page.






December 2024

New permanent plot at Siloam, New Caledonia
MELANOBS partners from the Environment Department of the Loyalty Islands Province and the AMAP lab, with the help of locals, set up the first 1-ha MELANOBS permanent forest plot in New Caledonia at Siloam, on the island of Lifou. See the Siloam plot page.






November 2024

First permanent plot at Nusumetu, Vanuatu
MELANOBS partners from the Vanuatu Department of Forestry and the AMAP lab, with the great help of the Nusumetu community, set up the project’s first 1-ha permanent forest plot at Nusumetu, on the island of Tanna, Vanuatu. See the Nusumetu plot page.






April 2024

Kick-off workshop in New Caledonia
Partners from across Melanesia and beyond spent a week together in Nouméa, New Caledonia (15–19 April 2024), to co-design and launch the MELANOBS network.

MELANOBS est coordonné par Thomas Ibanez, chargé de recherche à l’Institut de recherche pour le développement (IRD) et membre du laboratoire AMAP. Il est basé à Nouméa, en Nouvelle-Calédonie.

Il travaille surtout en Nouvelle-Calédonie et en Mélanésie. Au sein de MELANOBS, il coordonne le réseau régional de partenaires et pilote les parcelles permanentes de Nouvelle-Calédonie.

title: Parcelles permanentes
text:
Accueil | À propos | Parcelles permanentes | Herbiers | Actualités | Données | Publications | Contact | English




Arbre étiqueté dans la parcelle permanente de Vago, avec son point de mesure peint en jaune et un dendromètre à ruban manuel. Crédit photo : Thomas Ibanez



Le réseau MELANOBS est constitué de parcelles permanentes de 1 ha (100 m × 100 m). Dans chaque parcelle, toutes les tiges dont le diamètre à hauteur de poitrine (DHP, mesuré à 1,3 m du sol) atteint au moins 10 cm sont identifiées botaniquement, mesurées et cartographiées. Cela comprend les arbres mais aussi les palmiers, les fougères arborescentes, les pandanus et les autres formes de croissance. Chaque individu porte une étiquette avec un numéro unique, et le point de mesure est marqué à la peinture afin que chaque inventaire mesure la tige exactement à la même hauteur.
Le réseau cible les forêts tropicales humides de basse altitude. L’emplacement des parcelles est choisi avec les partenaires locaux, de préférence dans des zones protégées et accessibles.
Un échantillon de référence de chaque espèce recensée dans les parcelles a été récolté et déposé dans les herbiers de la région. Pour chaque espèce, le nom scientifique et les noms vernaculaires locaux sont relevés, afin que les données documentent aussi les savoirs locaux sur la flore.
Des mesures complémentaires sont réalisées dans et autour des parcelles, notamment la hauteur des arbres (H) et la densité du bois. Elles servent à calibrer des allométries locales hauteur–diamètre (H–DHP) et à estimer la biomasse aérienne et les stocks de carbone.
Les parcelles sont réinventoriées chaque année lorsque c’est possible, et au moins tous les cinq ans, afin de mesurer les taux de croissance, de mortalité et de recrutement des arbres, ainsi que l’évolution de la composition floristique. Par ailleurs, certains arbres sont équipés de dendromètres à ruban manuels (EMS DB20) afin de mesurer leur croissance plus précisément.
Le protocole suit les standards internationaux du réseau ForestPlots.net.



La parcelle permanente du parc provincial de la Rivière Bleue. À gauche : vue de la canopée montrant les limites de la parcelle et de ses sous-parcelles de 10 m × 10 m. À droite : arbres cartographiés, la taille des points étant proportionnelle au DHP et leur couleur indiquant la croissance secondaire entre 2025 et 2026.

title: Great Ferns Provincial Park
text:
Description
The Great Ferns permanent plot lies in the Great Ferns Provincial Park, on a gentle slope with volcano-sedimentary soils in the centre of the island of Grande Terre. The park is managed by the South Province. The plot was set up in September 2025 at about 380 m elevation and resurveyed in September 2026. The forest was logged until the 1970s and has been protected since 2008. It shows signs of disturbance by introduced deer (Rusa timorensis).
The most abundant tree species are Xylopia vieillardii (Annonaceae), Diospyros samoensis (Ebenaceae) and Calophyllum caledonicum (Calophyllaceae). The largest tree is an Agathis moorei (Araucariaceae) and the tallest is a Planchonella sphaerocarpa (Sapotaceae).

title: Nusumetu
text:
Description
The Nusumetu permanent plot lies in the Nusumetu community-managed conservation area at Green Hills, in the north of the island of Tanna. The area has been officially protected since 2024. The plot was set up in November 2024 at about 280 m elevation. The forest was heavily disturbed in the past by cattle roaming through it, and more recently by Tropical Cyclone Pam (2015).
The most abundant tree species are Didymocheton aneityensis (Meliaceae), Macaranga dioica (Euphorbiaceae) and Elaeocarpus angustifolius (Elaeocarpaceae), locally known as tuwai, naoula and niamiafil, respectively. The largest trees are banyans, Ficus prolixa (Moraceae), locally known as napuk.

title: Blue River Provincial Park
text:
Description
The Blue River permanent plot lies in the Blue River Provincial Park, on an alluvial flat with ultramafic soils in the south of the island of Grande Terre. The park is managed by the South Province. The plot was set up in March 2025 at about 180 m elevation and resurveyed in March 2026. The forest was logged until the late 1950s and has been protected since 1980. It still shows traces of past logging, as well as a large gap probably created by a tropical storm or cyclone.
The most abundant tree species are Codia jaffrei (Cunoniaceae), Archidendropsis granulosa (Fabaceae) and Plerandra gabriellae (Araliaceae). The largest and tallest tree is a Didymocheton rufescens (Meliaceae).
The plot lies within a larger 90 ha canopy observatory that is regularly surveyed by drone as part of the CanObs project.

title: MELANOBS
text:
Melanesian forests cover more than three-quarters of the region’s land, harbour a unique biodiversity and support local livelihoods, yet they face growing threats and remain little studied. MELANOBS brings together researchers and experts from across Melanesia and beyond to work on the ecology and conservation of these forests. The project rests on two pillars: a network of permanent forest plots in the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji and New Caledonia, and collaboration between the herbaria of the region. Learn more about the project →

title: Vanuatu National Herbarium
text:
Description
The Vanuatu National Herbarium (PVNH) originated in the 1970s and is managed by the Department of Forestry. It holds about 20,000 specimens, mostly from Vanuatu, with some from Fiji. The herbarium moved into new facilities in 2014, but the building was affected by the December 2024 earthquake and now needs to be extended.
The specimens are databased but not yet digitised. A first checklist of the vascular flora of Vanuatu, listing 1,631 species, was published in 2022 (Plunkett et al. 2022).

title: South Pacific Regional Herbarium
text:
Description
The South Pacific Regional Herbarium (SUVA), now part of the South Pacific Regional Herbarium and Biodiversity Centre, is managed by the University of the South Pacific through its Institute of Applied Sciences in Suva. It was founded in 1933 as the Fiji Herbarium, and the university took over its management in 1982. It holds about 90,000 specimens from Fiji and many other Pacific islands, including Nauru, New Caledonia, Norfolk Island, Pitcairn, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga and Vanuatu.
Most specimens are databased and about 20,000 have been digitised. The checklist of Fijian plant species, based on Flora Vitiensis Nova (A.C. Smith, 1979–1996), needs to be updated.

Description
The Solomon Islands National Herbarium (BSIP) was created in the 1960s and is managed by the Ministry of Forestry and Research. After its building was damaged in the 1990s and the collection was neglected for about a decade, some 25,000 specimens were sent to the South Pacific Regional Herbarium (SUVA) for safekeeping; they have since been returned. The herbarium has had new facilities since 2017 and holds about 50,000 specimens.
Databasing still needs to be improved, and the specimens have not yet been digitised. No checklist of Solomon Islands plant species has been published so far.

title: Herbarium of New Caledonia
text:
Description
The Herbarium of New Caledonia (NOU) is located at the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD) centre in Nouméa and is managed by UMR AMAP. It was refurbished in 2024, almost doubling its floor area. It holds about 100,000 specimens representing about 7,000 species. Most specimens come from New Caledonia, but the collection also includes many specimens from Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna, as well as some from Fiji and the Solomon Islands.
All specimens are databased, digitised at high resolution and available online. The checklist of New Caledonian plant species is regularly updated through Florical (Morat et al. 2012).

title: Poitete
text:
Description
The Poitete permanent plot lies in the Tekolea Forest Reserve (whose name means “leave it alone” or “do not disturb”), near the Poitete forestry campus of Solomon Islands National University, in the north of the island of Kolombangara. The plot was set up in May 2025 at about 110 m elevation. The forest was logged until the late 1980s.
The most abundant tree species are Neoscortechinia forbesii (Euphorbiaceae), locally known as kerosene wood, Aporosa papuana (Phyllanthaceae) and Prasoxylon cf. alliaceum (Meliaceae), locally known as ai mok’ta’a. The largest tree is a Pometia pinnata (Sapindaceae), locally known as gema or qema, and the tallest is a Terminalia calamansanai (Combretaceae), locally known as sapeqava.

Description
The Vago permanent plot lies in the Vago Forest Reserve, a protected area established in 1959 north of Suva, on the island of Viti Levu. The plot was set up in July 2026 on a gentle slope at about 220 m elevation. The forest shows no obvious signs of recent disturbance.
The most abundant tree species include Haplolobus floribundus (Burseraceae), locally known as kaunigai, and Myristica species (Myristicaceae), locally known as kaudamu. The largest tree is a Parinari insularum (Chrysobalanaceae), locally known as sa, and the tallest is an Agathis macrophylla (Araucariaceae), locally known as dakua makadre.

Description
The Siloam permanent plot lies on the land of the Siloam tribu, on uplifted coral limestone in the north of the island of Lifou. The plot was set up in December 2024 at about 60 m elevation and resurveyed in December 2025. The forest shows no obvious signs of recent disturbance.
The most abundant tree species are Aglaia elaeagnoidea (Meliaceae), Diospyros calciphila (Ebenaceae) and Alectryon carinatum (Sapindaceae), locally known as sö, xetr and cangen, respectively. The largest tree is an Elaeodendron curtipendulum (Celastraceae), locally known as thidraxep, and the tallest is an Aglaia elaeagnoidea, reaching only about 20 m.

title: Permanent plots
text:
Tagged tree in the Vago permanent plot, with its point of measurement painted in yellow and a manual band dendrometer. Photo: Thomas Ibanez



The MELANOBS network is made up of permanent plots of 1 ha (100 m × 100 m). In each plot, every stem with a diameter at breast height (DBH, measured 1.3 m above the ground) of at least 10 cm is identified botanically, measured and mapped. This includes trees as well as palms, tree ferns, pandanus and other growth forms. Each individual carries a tag with a unique number, and the point of measurement is marked with paint so that every census measures the stem at exactly the same height.
The network focuses on lowland tropical wet forest. Plot locations are chosen together with local partners, preferably in protected and accessible areas.
A voucher specimen of each species recorded in the plots has been collected and deposited in the herbaria of the region. For each species, both the scientific name and the local vernacular names are recorded, so that the data also document local knowledge of the flora.
Additional measurements are made in and around the plots, including tree height (H) and wood density. They are used to calibrate local height–diameter (H–DBH) allometries and to estimate above-ground biomass and carbon stocks.
The plots are resurveyed every year where possible, and at least every five years, to measure tree growth, mortality and recruitment rates, as well as changes in species composition. In addition, some trees are fitted with manual band dendrometers (EMS DB20) to measure their growth more accurately.
The protocol follows the international standards of the ForestPlots.net network.



The Blue River Provincial Park permanent plot. Left: canopy view showing the border of the plot and its 10 m × 10 m subplots. Right: mapped trees, with point size proportional to DBH and colour showing secondary growth rate between 2025 and 2026.

Les forêts mélanésiennes couvrent plus des trois quarts des terres de la région, abritent une biodiversité unique et font vivre les populations locales, mais elles sont de plus en plus menacées et restent peu étudiées. MELANOBS réunit des chercheurs et des experts de Mélanésie et d’ailleurs autour de l’écologie et de la conservation de ces forêts. Le projet repose sur deux piliers : un réseau de parcelles forestières permanentes aux Îles Salomon, au Vanuatu, aux Fidji et en Nouvelle-Calédonie, et la collaboration entre les herbiers de la région. title: À propos
text:
La Mélanésie




Terminalia calamansanai (Combretaceae), l’espèce d’arbre la plus haute de la parcelle permanente de Poitete, Îles Salomon. Crédit photo : Ghislain Vieilledent



La Mélanésie est une sous-région géographique et culturelle du Pacifique Sud-Ouest, composée de milliers d’îles situées entre l’équateur et le tropique du Capricorne. Du nord-ouest au sud-est, elle comprend les provinces indonésiennes de l’ouest de la Nouvelle-Guinée, les États indépendants de Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée, des Îles Salomon, du Vanuatu et des Fidji, ainsi que la Nouvelle-Calédonie, territoire français.
Les forêts couvrent plus des trois quarts des terres de Mélanésie. Elles abritent une biodiversité unique et contribuent à atténuer le réchauffement climatique en stockant du carbone. Elles sont aussi essentielles au bien-être des populations locales, en particulier en milieu rural, grâce aux nombreux services écosystémiques qu’elles rendent. Dans le contexte des changements globaux, ces forêts font face à de multiples menaces : conversion en terres agricoles, exploitation forestière, activités minières, incendies, cyclones, espèces envahissantes et changement climatique. Malgré leur importance et leur vulnérabilité potentielle, elles restent relativement peu étudiées.
La communauté scientifique locale travaillant sur l’écologie et la conservation des forêts mélanésiennes est réduite et géographiquement dispersée. Chercheurs et experts travaillent souvent de manière isolée, avec peu d’échanges entre pays, alors qu’ils font face à des problèmes similaires : gérer les effets des changements globaux en milieu insulaire, avec des effectifs et une expertise limités pour relever les défis de la conservation.

title: À propos
text:
Objectifs
MELANOBS, l’observatoire mélanésien de la réponse des forêts aux changements globaux, est une réponse régionale à ces défis, qui associe collaboration et recherche au service de la conservation des forêts et des communautés mélanésiennes. Le projet vise à construire un réseau international de chercheurs et d’experts travaillant sur l’écologie et la conservation des forêts mélanésiennes, fondé sur la collaboration, le renforcement des capacités et l’équité.
Plus précisément, il vise à :

renforcer les capacités grâce à des partenariats de recherche ;
améliorer les connaissances sur la biodiversité forestière, par exemple en établissant des listes d’espèces à l’échelle de chaque île ;
améliorer les connaissances sur le fonctionnement des forêts, par exemple en suivant la démographie des arbres (croissance, mortalité et recrutement).

Le projet repose sur deux piliers : l’installation et le suivi d’un réseau de parcelles forestières permanentes, et le renforcement de la collaboration entre les herbiers de la région.

title: À propos
text:
Partenaires
MELANOBS réunit des partenaires aux profils variés : des organismes de recherche et universités (l’unité mixte de recherche AMAP, l’Université nationale des Îles Salomon, l’Université du Pacifique Sud, Adelaide University et le Jardin botanique de New York), des ONG (Endemia et NatureFiji-MareqetiViti) et des administrations (le ministère des Forêts et de la Recherche des Îles Salomon, le département des Forêts du Vanuatu, le ministère de la Pêche et des Forêts des Fidji et, en Nouvelle-Calédonie, la direction de l’Environnement de la province des îles Loyauté et le service de gestion des aires protégées de la province Sud). Parmi eux figurent les conservateurs des herbiers de la région.



Les partenaires de MELANOBS lors de l’atelier de lancement du projet en Nouvelle-Calédonie (avril 2024). De gauche à droite : Presley Dovo (département des Forêts, Vanuatu), Mereia Tabua (NatureFiji-MareqetiViti, Fidji), Marika Tuiwawa (Université du Pacifique Sud, Fidji), Ghislain Vieilledent (CIRAD, UMR AMAP, Nouvelle-Calédonie), David Bruy (IRD, UMR AMAP, Nouvelle-Calédonie), Alivereti Naikatini (ministère des Forêts, Fidji), Gunnar Keppel (Adelaide University, Australie), Willie Lore (département des Forêts, Vanuatu), Patrick Nimiago (PNG Forest Research Institute, Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée), Thomas Ibanez (IRD, UMR AMAP, Nouvelle-Calédonie), Eric Katovai (Université nationale des Îles Salomon), Pagi Toko (Binatang Research Center, Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée), Myknee Sirikolo (ministère des Forêts et de la Recherche, Îles Salomon). title: À propos
text:
Financeurs
La première phase de MELANOBS a été financée par l’Institut de recherche pour le développement (IRD) et par le ministère de l’Europe et des Affaires étrangères (MEAE), au titre du Fonds Pacifique pour la coopération régionale.
L’installation et le réinventaire des parcelles en Nouvelle-Calédonie ont également été soutenus par l’Agence nationale de la recherche (ANR) dans le cadre du PEPR FORESTT (projet MONITOR).

title: About
text:
Terminalia calamansanai (Combretaceae), the tallest tree species in the Poitete permanent plot, Solomon Islands. Photo: Ghislain Vieilledent



Melanesia is a geographic and cultural subregion of the southwest Pacific, made up of thousands of islands lying between the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn. From northwest to southeast, it includes the Indonesian provinces of western New Guinea, the independent states of Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and Fiji, and the French territory of New Caledonia.
Forests cover more than three-quarters of the land in Melanesia. They support a unique biodiversity and help mitigate global warming by storing carbon. They are also essential to the well-being of local people, particularly in rural areas, through the many ecosystem services they provide. In the context of global change, these forests face multiple threats, including conversion to agricultural land, logging, mining, fires, cyclones, invasive species and climate change. Despite their importance and potential vulnerability, they remain relatively little studied.
The local scientific community working on the ecology and conservation of Melanesian forests is small and geographically dispersed. Researchers and experts often work in isolation, with little exchange between countries, even though they face similar problems: managing the effects of global change in island environments, with limited staff and expertise to meet conservation challenges.

title: About
text:
Aims
MELANOBS, the Melanesian Observatory of forest responses to global change, is a regional response to these challenges, combining collaboration and research to support forest conservation for the benefit of Melanesian communities. The project aims to build an international network of researchers and experts working on the ecology and conservation of Melanesian forests, based on collaboration, capacity building and equity.
More specifically, it seeks to:

build capacity through research partnerships;
improve knowledge of forest biodiversity, for example by establishing species checklists at the island level;
improve knowledge of forest functioning, for example by monitoring tree demography (growth, mortality and recruitment).

The project rests on two pillars: establishing and maintaining a network of permanent forest plots, and strengthening collaboration between the herbaria of the region.

title: About
text:
Partners
MELANOBS brings together partners from a range of backgrounds: research and academic institutions (the AMAP joint research unit, Solomon Islands National University, the University of the South Pacific, Adelaide University and the New York Botanical Garden), NGOs (Endemia and NatureFiji-MareqetiViti) and government agencies (the Solomon Islands Ministry of Forestry and Research, the Vanuatu Department of Forestry, the Fiji Ministry of Fisheries and Forestry and, in New Caledonia, the Environment Department of the Loyalty Islands Province and the Protected Areas Management Department of the South Province). Among them are the curators of the region’s herbaria.

title: About
text:
Funders
The first phase of MELANOBS was funded by the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD) and by the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs (MEAE), through the Pacific Fund for regional cooperation.
The establishment and resurveys of the plots in New Caledonia were also supported by the French National Research Agency (ANR) through the PEPR FORESTT programme (MONITOR project).
